title: Nepal’s flood has reignited the climate reparations debate
gist: A half-kilometre glacier cliff sheared off Langtang Lirung on 26th August 2026, fell 1,200m, registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake and sent a debris flow 100km at 193km/h, killing 1,287 with 5,000+ missing, flattening 12 hydro plants and 10 per cent of Nepal's generation capacity. Smedley argues the disaster exposes a loss-and-damage fund holding $631m against a stated need of $100bn–$580bn a year, and predicts reparations will dominate Cop31 in Turkey.

insights.claim: On 26th August 2026 a section of glacier cliff over half a kilometre wide sheared off the north face of Langtang Lirung, fell 1,200 metres in seconds, registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake on impact and triggered a debris flow that travelled 100km down the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi valleys at an average 193km per hour.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Establishes a new class of high-energy Himalayan hazard whose speed and scale defeat existing warning systems and infrastructure siting assumptions.
insights.locator: When a section of glacier cliff over half a kilometre wide

insights.claim: Nepal's early warning system relied on river level-gauges that register flash floods but not 80m-high mudflows and boulders the size of houses, so many people had no time to reach safety.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Adaptation infrastructure calibrated to the last disaster fails against the next one — a systematic underestimation in climate-resilience budgeting.
insights.locator: Nepal’s early warning system relied on a network of river level-gauges

insights.claim: Confirmed deaths stand at 1,287 with more than 5,000 still missing at the time of writing.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: The human scale is what gives Nepal's compensation claim diplomatic weight at Cop31.
insights.locator: At the time of writing, 1,287 people are confirmed dead

insights.claim: Permafrost is the mechanism: Langtang Lirung's high slopes are held together by frozen ground that weakens as it warms, while meltwater seeps into rock cracks and prises them wider each time it refreezes — and satellite imagery showed considerable snowmelt in the days before the collapse.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A named physical mechanism with satellite-observable precursors, meaning this hazard class is in principle monitorable and insurable.
insights.quote: As that frozen ground warms and ice inside thaws
insights.locator: Langtang Lirung’s high mountain slopes are held together by permafrost

insights.claim: The Himalayan region as a whole is warming 50 per cent faster than the global average, and ice loss rates across the Hindu Kush have roughly doubled since 2000.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Regional amplification of this size means Himalayan hazard frequency will rise faster than global climate models imply — material for South Asian infrastructure and hydro assets.
insights.locator: The Himalayan region as a whole is warming 50 per cent faster

insights.claim: A recent study found the Langtang region warmed by 0.31°C every decade between 1960 and 2023, and July 2026 was its second warmest July while August up to the collapse was the warmest ever.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Localised warming plus record antecedent months is the pattern to screen for when assessing other glaciated basins.
insights.locator: A recent study of the Langtang region found

insights.claim: The Yala glacier had shrunk by 66 per cent since the 1970s and was memorialised in a Buddhist ceremony with plaques on 12th May 2025, months before the disaster struck close to the same site.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Documented glacier retreat preceded the catastrophic failure — retreat metrics are a usable leading indicator of slope instability.
insights.locator: In Langtang, Nepal, a group of locals and glaciologists

insights.claim: The event is explicitly not a freak: it follows smaller floods in 2016, 2021 and 2024 that were also caused in part by rapid warming.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Recurrence is already established — this should be modelled as an increasing-frequency hazard, not a tail event.
insights.locator: This was no freak event

insights.claim: The Nepali Times editorial argued nothing about the disaster was natural — not the glacier melting from fossil-fuel greenhouse gas buildup, not the siting of expensive hydropower plants on trans-Himalayan rivers, not designing highways to follow rivers, not the settlements around them, not the corruption and poor governance.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Attribution to siting and governance choices, not just emissions, is what exposes domestic planning and construction decisions to liability.
insights.locator: An editorial in the Nepali Times noted

insights.claim: Nepal had invested more than £6.7bn building hydropower dams across its rivers, and August's disaster flattened 12 hydroelectric plants, eradicating 10 per cent of the country's total energy generation capacity.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A single event destroyed a tenth of national generation capacity — a concrete warning on concentration risk for run-of-river hydro in glaciated basins.
insights.locator: Nepal had invested more than £6.7bn in building hydropower dams

insights.claim: More than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt and Kathmandu estimates recovery costs at more than $5bn, roughly 10 per cent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A 10-per-cent-of-GDP reconstruction bill for a low-income state is a sovereign financing event, not a humanitarian line item.
insights.locator: More than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt

insights.claim: Despite the compensation push, Nepal still needs traditional aid, which foreign minister Shisir Khanal has put at a relatively modest $20m.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: The gap between a $20m immediate aid ask and a $5bn recovery bill shows why reparations, not aid, is the framing Nepal has adopted.
insights.locator: To cover these costs, Nepal still needs traditional aid

insights.claim: Nepal's foreign minister said the country will focus less on aid and more on “justice and compensation”, framing it as a matter of legal and moral liability and naming China, the United States and India as the top three emitters with a historical responsibility to compensate.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A vulnerable state explicitly reframing climate finance as liability rather than charity — the doctrinal shift that would open the door to climate litigation against major emitters.
insights.quote: This is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability.
insights.locator: In the aftermath of the flood, Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal

insights.claim: The author argues loss and damage should become the third pillar of UN climate diplomacy alongside mitigation and adaptation, a position set out in a 2025 book co-authored with the UN's Climate Vulnerability Forum and the V20 group.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: If loss and damage becomes a formal third pillar, climate negotiations acquire a transfer-payment axis with real fiscal consequences for developed states.
insights.locator: In a 2025 book I co-authored

insights.claim: Among seasoned Cop negotiators the scale of compensation is still hotly debated and the “R” word, reparation, is fiercely resisted.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Language resistance marks the real negotiating line — expect compensation to be delivered under any label except reparations.
insights.locator: Seasoned Cop negotiators and UN observers acknowledged

insights.claim: Against a stated need of $100bn–$580bn a year, the entire loss and damage fund established at Cop27 sits at $631m, with only around $350m actually available for reparations and the rest going to running costs.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A fund capitalised at roughly 0.1 per cent of low-end need is functionally symbolic — the credibility gap that will define Cop31.
insights.locator: Compared to a stated need of $100bn-$580bn a year

insights.claim: The UK, the fifth largest historical carbon emitter, has contributed $50m to the fund, while in 2025 the United States withdrew from the loss and damage fund agreement entirely and cut overseas aid including the disaster response team that might once have supported Nepal.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Donor retrenchment is happening exactly as claims accelerate, widening the gap that vulnerable states will try to close through litigation and diplomatic leverage.
insights.locator: towards which the UK (the fifth largest historical carbon emitter)

insights.claim: Requests into the UN loss and damage fund already amount to $2.8bn, nearly eight times what is available, and that was before the Nepal disaster.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Claims are already 8x capacity — rationing and political conflict over allocation are guaranteed.
insights.locator: Requests into the UN loss and damage fund already amount

insights.claim: Eight members of the UN's Fund for responding to Loss and Damage representing Africa, Asia and the least developed countries have called for an extraordinary meeting on Nepal's appeal, seeing it as a test of whether the fund can act fast when it matters.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A near-term, observable test of the fund's operational credibility — failure would accelerate the shift to litigation-based claims.
insights.quote: a test of whether the fund can act fast when it matters
insights.locator: According to the Lowy Institute, a thinktank

insights.claim: An economist at the Maldives Finance Ministry told the author that accessing any climate financing, including the UN loss and damage fund, was almost impossible, and that remains the case.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Access friction, not just capitalisation, is the binding constraint — disbursement mechanics are where climate finance actually fails.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, an economist at the Maldives Finance Ministry

insights.claim: A senior UN source who has witnessed many disasters says he is still having nightmares from the videos and now expects loss and damage to shoot up the agenda at Cop31 in Turkey in November.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: A dated catalyst: Cop31 in Turkey in November is where loss-and-damage financing is most likely to be renegotiated.
insights.locator: A senior UN source, who has witnessed many disasters
